challenge_responses.response: Accepted via the qualifier route offered as the first of two alternatives in the suggested_action, rather than the merge route. The three-way inconsistency is real, but the fix is not to reprice 2:1 — it is to state, identically in decisions 001, 005, and 015, the two-part test that a bare verse-initial disjunctive clause has always been implicitly satisfying without being named: (1) does the clause introduce a participant genuinely new to the story, ahead of that participant's own scene, rather than merely naming a participant a preceding roster has already inventoried; and (2) does it carry a temporal deictic placing the narrating voice outside story-time. Ruth 1:2 fails test (1) and is rightly absorbed into decision 001 with no seam of its own. Ruth 2:1 passes test (1) alone — Boaz is wholly new to the story and his introduction runs well ahead of his actual entrance at 2:4 — earning a real but modest seam. I tested the alternative of separating the two neighbor-women's speeches (vv14-15, v17) from Naomi's nursing gesture (v16) and agree with the rejection, with one addition: the women are called הַנָּשִׁים at v14 and הַשְּׁכֵנוֹת ('the neighbor-women') at v17, a designation shift that could in principle suggest a different group, but this reads as ordinary Hebrew narrative variation for the same referent — townswomen generally, then specified as neighbors for the intimate naming scene — rather than a participant-set change, so it doesn't support a further split. Refusing to slice the register internally is right too, a begetting chain meaning nothing until it arrives at the last name. What I contest is one factual assertion inside the rationale. The heading is said to be used elsewhere in the canon exclusively to launch genealogical registers. It is not, and the counterexamples are not marginal: the same formula heads the account of the heavens and the earth, the Isaac section that narrates Jacob and Esau, and the Jacob section that runs on into the Joseph story.
